title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit to evaluate whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality, fuzzy 5‑gram overlap, provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered guarded exclusions changes validator‑measured success rates. The run used a single hosted LLM (declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini), deterministic task generation, and a deterministic NetOps validator. Execution completed 300 episodes (150 item pairs) but, because no high‑confidence contamination flags occurred and independent_condition_generation was set to false, each item used a single shared generation for both baseline and guarded conditions (model_calls_used = 150). The validator returned pass for all episodes (baseline 150/150; guarded 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Critically, archived execution facts show the sample was provenance‑stable synthetic and that shared generation semantics produced identical outputs per item; these two facts mechanistically explain the degenerate null outcome and bound the audit's inferential scope. We reconcile the preregistration and execution artifacts, report deterministic reconciliation and validator traces, and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations (provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation, multi‑model scope, paraphrase‑sensitive detectors, and per‑item detector logging) to increase audit sensitivity in future contamination assessments.

sections.introduction:
Motivation and problem statement. Large language models (LLMs) are now applied to operational NetOps tasks (intent→configuration, automated repair). Benchmarks drive claims about LLM capability, but two evaluation risks can inflate apparent performance: dataset contamination (benchmark items appearing, wholly or partially, in model training corpora) and construct invalidity (templated, low‑complexity tasks that do not reflect real operational difficulty). Both problems threaten operational trust in LLM‑driven NetOps workflows and motivate contamination‑aware, oracle‑backed audits that can be reproduced and verified from archived artifacts.

Research question and scope. We preregistered an auditable confirmatory study to answer: under conservative deterministic contamination detectors (canonical exact‑match; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance timestamp heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy, (1) how many high‑confidence flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and (2) how much does applying those controls change validator‑measured success rates? The design specified paired comparisons (baseline vs guarded) across item×model pairs with a deterministic NetOps validator as the functional oracle. Important scope boundary: the executed sample used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks and shared‑generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). Those execution facts are archived and materially limit inferences about contamination in web‑sourced public benchmarks; we make that limitation explicit here.
sections.related_work:
LLMs for NetOps and validate–repair pipelines. Recent system and benchmark work shows LLMs can generate useful device configurations and propose repairs; integrating deterministic or formal validators and iterative repair loops improves average repair quality compared to unchecked generation. Representative tool and systems work demonstrates that header‑space–style formal analyzers and localized subspecification approaches are practical oracles for reachability/policy checks and are suitable verification backends for generate–validate architectures.

Evaluation validity, contamination, and meta‑audits. Meta‑evaluations across LLM benchmarks document contamination and construct‑validity risks and recommend contamination detectors, provenance tracing, and preplanned exclusion/repair policies. Our preregistration implements a conservative subset of such defenses (exact canonical equality, fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80, and provenance timestamp heuristics) and pairs those detectors with deterministic replacement rules and validator‑backed scoring. Unlike broad capability benchmarks, the present study focuses on whether these preregistered controls would have altered validator outcomes in a reproducible execution regime.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. We preregistered the study as contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) across item×model pairs. The confirmatory test is an exact two‑sided McNemar test; we additionally compute a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval using 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) as specified in the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor.

Detectors and guarded policy (preregistered). Detectors: (1) exact normalized token equality after canonicalization; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap (Jaccard/overlap) with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 and sensitivity thresholds 0.65 and 0.50; and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item timestamps to the model's public cutoff. Guarded policy: deterministically exclude only high‑confidence flagged items (exact match OR fuzzy overlap ≥ 0.80) and replace them by deterministic retemplating/topology augmentation from the same generator distribution using fixed seeds; replacements must meet an embedding‑similarity constraint and pass validator checks before acceptance. These rules were frozen in the preregistration and implemented in the transformation_manifest archived with the run.

Sampling, generation semantics, and validators. The preregistration allowed deterministic task generators and permitted shared generation semantics; execution used deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 to produce synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:"). Execution parameters set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics): when no high‑confidence exclusions occurred a single shared generation per item was reused for both baseline and guarded episodes. The verification oracle was deterministic_netops_validator_v5; its scoring rule for intent→configuration tasks is full_intent_constraint_validation (generated configuration must reach the intended final state and adhere to workflow constraints). Validator traces include parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, final_state, and violation codes and are archived for each episode.

Planned analyses and sensitivity plan. The primary confirmatory test follows the preregistration. Prespecified sensitivity analyses included (a) treating failed model calls as failures (missingness handling), (b) fuzzy thresholds at 0.50 and 0.65 in addition to 0.80, and (c) subgrouping by templated vs realistic items using a templating detector. The preregistration included power guidance targeting a multi‑model design to detect ≈5 percentage‑point paired differences at 80% power; the single‑model single‑call execution reduces detectable effect size and power—this tradeoff is acknowledged and quantified in Results and Discussion.

Operationalized reproducibility measures. All sampling seeds, generator identifiers, validator versions, model declaration, execution logs, and raw responses were archived. The execution manifest records start/completion timestamps, completed episodes, and model_calls_used. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts ensure episode accounting consistency and are available in the archived bundle. For transparency, per‑episode validator traces and the paired contingency table were recorded; summary artifacts exist for condition counts and missingness. Where preregistered detectors would have produced per‑item overlap scores, the archived detector workflow recorded detailed overlap outputs only for flagged episodes or for replacement operations; because no high‑confidence flags occurred in this run no per‑item overlap distribution artifact was generated for reporting in the main text—this absence is explicitly documented in Results.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and basic outcomes. Execution completed planned_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 item pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item). Deterministic_reconciliation confirms complete_pair_count = 150 and consistent provider call accounting.

Contamination detector outcomes. Under the preregistered detectors and thresholds, execution produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags (analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty of flagged rows). The archived detector logs show no replacement operations were invoked. Because the detector workflow archived detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs only for episodes reaching flagging thresholds or replacement handling, the run contains no archived distribution summary of fuzzy overlaps to report; we therefore report the artifact‑verifiable fact that no high‑confidence flags occurred and no replacements were performed.

Validator outcomes and confirmatory statistics. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scored all baseline episodes as pass (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and all guarded episodes as pass (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) = 0.0 percentage points. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All per‑episode validator traces and the paired contingency artifact are archived.

Representative exemplar episode. A representative archived episode (pair‑000001 / task‑000001) illustrates the structure of task payload, shared_initial_candidate content, raw response, and validator trace. For task‑000001 the reference answer and normalized_response are identical and the validator returned score = 1 (score_reason_code = VALID_CONFIGURATION), parsed_command_count = 4, and final_state matching the intent. This exemplar and its traces are archived and referenced in the execution manifest.

Why the outcome is degenerate: artifact‑grounded explanation. Two execution facts explain the degenerate null result. First, the confirmatory sample comprised provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (source_identifier: "synthetic-netops:"), so canonical exact matches to public corpus fingerprints and high fuzzy 5‑gram overlaps above the preregistered high‑confidence threshold did not occur. Second, independent_condition_generation was false (shared_initial_candidate semantics), so when exclusions were absent a single shared model generation per item was reused for baseline and guarded episodes. Because these two facts are recorded in the archived model_configuration.json and task_manifest.jsonl, they mechanistically produced identical baseline and guarded outputs per item and thus made the paired test uninformative for generation‑level contamination detection in this run.

Sensitivity and power interpretation. The preregistration's power guidance targeted multi‑model designs to detect ~5 percentage‑point paired differences at 80% power. Under the executed single‑model, shared‑generation regime, observable discordance is constrained to cases where detectors would have excluded and replaced items; absence of exclusions in this synthetic sample therefore reduces power to detect generation‑level contamination effects to effectively zero. This is an execution‑documented limitation rather than an analytical failure: the artifacts show that the preregistered rules were applied and no flags triggered, and the resulting paired statistics follow deterministically from that execution path.
sections.discussion:
What the execution does and does not show. The archived evidence supports one narrowly scoped conclusion: for this reproducible, provenance‑stable synthetic sample and under conservative deterministic detectors, no preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags arose and guarded exclusions did not change validator outcomes (baseline = guarded = 150/150). The execution does not show that public web‑sourced benchmarks are contamination‑free, nor does it validate the detectors' sensitivity to paraphrased or partial leakage. We explicitly avoid extrapolation beyond the recorded artifacts.

Design lessons and recommended audit improvements (artifact‑grounded). The preregistration→execution reconciliation suggests concrete, artifact‑supported design changes to increase audit sensitivity: (1) sample provenance‑rich public items (web archives, DOI‑referenced material) rather than synthetic tasks to exercise detector sensitivity to real training‑corpus leakage; (2) set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded conditions are produced by independent generations and cannot collapse to a shared output; (3) expand to multi‑model and multiple‑seed sampling to allow cross‑model contamination signals; (4) always log per‑item fuzzy overlap scores (not only flagged cases) so auditors can report overlap distributions and threshold distances; and (5) introduce paraphrase‑robust contamination detectors and a small human adjudication pipeline for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows from archived execution facts (task provenance, generation semantics, absence of per‑item overlap artifacts) as recorded in the execution_manifest and analysis artifacts.

Threats to validity and construct considerations. Internal validity: prompt sensitivity and generation semantics materially affect outcomes—shared generation collapses paired contrasts unless exclusions occur. Construct validity: the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 assesses a defined set of functional constraints (intent final state, workflow rules); passing the validator indicates satisfaction of those checks but does not guarantee production readiness or absence of regressions not encoded in the validator. External validity: single‑model (gpt‑5‑mini) and synthetic sampling limit generalizability to other LLMs and to public benchmark corpora. Conclusion validity: the paired test is informative only when per‑item independent generations or exclusions produce discordant outcomes; in our execution the test is degenerate by design and recorded artifacts reflect that.

Operational implications for NetOps evaluation practice. Audits intended to assess contamination in public benchmarks should prioritize provenance‑rich sampling, independent condition generation, and per‑item detector logging. Validator‑backed oracles remain valuable to measure functional correctness, but audit designs must ensure detector outputs are captured at sufficient granularity to support post‑hoc sensitivity analyses and adjudication.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed an artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors in an LLM‑for‑NetOps setting. For the executed provenance‑stable synthetic sample and shared‑generation semantics, no high‑confidence contamination flags occurred and validator pass rates were identical (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). Archived artifacts explain this degenerate outcome: synthetic provenance prevented detector matches and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics caused identical outputs across conditions. The run therefore answers the preregistered methodological question for this execution regime but does not address contamination prevalence in web‑sourced benchmarks. We provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations (provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation per condition, multi‑model scope, paraphrase‑sensitive detectors, and comprehensive per‑item detector logging) to increase audit sensitivity in future studies. All execution and analysis artifacts, per‑episode validator traces, execution manifests, and deterministic reconciliation artifacts were archived by the autonomous pipeline and are available in the execution bundle for verification.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items for this run were provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") — absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication.

Passing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
